Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics ER 2, a new model designed to serve as a high-level brain for robots, enabling real-time spatial reasoning, multi-step task orchestration, and collaboration among multiple robots. It supports calling external tools like Google Search and user-defined functions, enabling robots to plan and execute tasks while simultaneously thinking ahead. The model also introduces multi-robot collaboration capabilities, allowing robots to work together in shared spaces to complete workflows beyond the scope of individual robots.

This advancement addresses key challenges in robotics such as task completion verification and progress tracking through improved video understanding techniques. Gemini Robotics ER 2's capabilities have been demonstrated with Boston Dynamics' Spot robot, which can perform interactive tasks like fetching objects based on natural language commands. The model is publicly available for developers to integrate into robotic applications, marking a significant step forward in embodied AI for physical agents.

items.originalTitle: Prompt turns Microsoft Copilot into an AI worm
items.summary:
A security researcher has shown how Microsoft Copilot for Word can be exploited to create a self-spreading AI worm that silently modifies documents by embedding hidden JSON-formatted prompts as white text. When Copilot processes these documents, it reads the hidden instructions and propagates the malicious prompt into new files, enabling the worm to spread through normal document-sharing without using macros or traditional malware.

The attack persists despite Microsoft's mitigations, including updates to GPT-5.5 and 5.6 models, highlighting an architectural vulnerability in large language model systems where attacker-controlled content shares the same context window as trusted instructions. Users are advised to treat external documents as untrusted when using Copilot, review documents carefully, and consider disabling Copilot features to reduce risk.

items.originalTitle: Designing Docs for AI Agents
items.summary:
Jamdesk highlights a shift in documentation consumption from humans to AI agents, noting that agents crawl tens of thousands of pages per human visitor and prefer explicit, standalone content in markdown format over traditional HTML. The company argues that conventional human-focused documentation practices, such as progressive disclosure and navigation structures, hinder AI agents, which read entire documents at once and rely on up-to-date, precise information.

The article draws on data from Cloudflare and Chroma Research to show the scale of AI crawling and the challenges of context length for models. Jamdesk recommends designing docs with multiple access points like llms.txt and per-page markdown endpoints, treating error messages as key content, and avoiding large monolithic pages to prevent context degradation. This approach aims to optimize documentation for AI agents that increasingly serve as the primary audience for technical content.

items.title: Researchers say a fundamental flaw in large language models makes them inherently vulnerable to attacks that bypass safety measures [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack
items.summary:
A team of researchers presented a paper at the International Conference on Machine Learning arguing that large language models (LLMs) cannot be made fully secure due to a fundamental flaw in how they process instructions. This flaw allows attackers to trick LLMs into revealing restricted information or performing unsafe actions by manipulating how the models identify the source of instructions.

The researchers demonstrated attacks called chain-of-thought forgeries, which exploit the models' internal tagging system that distinguishes user input from system instructions and model-generated notes. By mimicking the model's internal reasoning style, attackers can cause LLMs to act on malicious prompts as if they originated from trusted sources. The vulnerability affects multiple popular models from companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Alibaba, and DeepSeek.

This discovery challenges current security approaches that rely on red-teaming and training models to resist known attacks, as no list of forbidden instructions can be exhaustive. The researchers warn that this issue may be fundamentally unsolvable, raising significant concerns about the safety of LLMs in applications ranging from government and military systems to healthcare and online services.

items.originalTitle: Show HN: Wasted Cycles – Local wall-clock profiler for AI coding agents
items.summary:
Wasted Cycles is a local profiling tool designed for AI coding agents that measures how much time is spent blocked on machine tasks versus active coding. It runs without installation, accounts, or data uploads by downloading a verified binary temporarily and analyzing JSONL trace files on the user's machine. The profiler categorizes time into agent working, blocked on compute, and human waiting, helping identify bottlenecks like repeated builds or tests and providing a live terminal interface for detailed analysis.

The tool supports multiple trace formats and reconstructs elapsed segments from timestamped events to classify activity precisely, avoiding false positives from pasted logs or prompts. It distinguishes between different types of idle time and repeated work, offering confidence scores for each segment. Wasted Cycles emphasizes privacy by never storing or uploading prompt text or source code, focusing solely on timestamps and coarse labels to provide actionable insights into AI coding workflows.

items.originalTitle: Meta Could Learn Cost Control From Microsoft
items.summary:
Talk about a tale of two companies. Today’s June-quarter earnings reports from Meta Platforms and Microsoft showed very different approaches to cost control, a discipline that may never be more important for big tech companies. Meta, whose CEO Mark Zuckerberg seems to have a you-only-live-once approach to AI investment, reported a 55% surge in operating expenses, which helped slash its operating income 8% in the quarter. (A bit of that cost growth was due to legal expenses and employee severance but even excluding those items, costs still rose 42%).

Meta’s free cash flow shriveled by 91% to a bit below $800 million, as capital expenditures nearly doubled to $30 billion—the equivalent of half Meta’s revenue. Microsoft’s numbers look quite different. The cloud and software giant is also spending a fortune on AI-related capex—$35.8 billion in the quarter, although that’s only 40% of its revenue. But Microsoft’s operating expenses rose only 10%. As a result, its operating income rose 18%, quite the contrast to Meta. Investors noticed: While Meta shares fell as much as 10% in after-hours trading, Microsoft stock gained 9%.
